title: MODULE 14 — Frontend Production Engineering and Industry Capstone

overview.text: Module objective: Combine everything learned throughout Modern Web & Frontend Engineering to design, develop, test, deploy, monitor and maintain a complete production-ready frontend application.
Previous modules focused on learning frontend technologies, programming concepts, browser APIs, application architecture, React development, API integration, performance, security and SEO.

This module moves from development to professional frontend engineering. Students will learn how real development teams prepare applications for production, maintain code quality, manage deployments, handle failures, support different devices and build software that can grow over time.
The module concludes with an industry-style capstone: building a complete Production-Ready Learning Management Platform.

blocks.text: Modern frontend applications contain JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, CSS, images, fonts, icons and other resources. Browsers cannot always use these development files directly in their original form. Build systems prepare these resources for browsers by processing, transforming, organizing and optimizing them.
1.1 Understanding the Frontend Build Process
A frontend build process transforms source code into deployable production assets (React JSX, JS modules, CSS/Tailwind, SVG/images, fonts, third-party libraries).

Pipeline: Source code collection -> Dependency resolution -> Module processing -> JSX and TypeScript transformation -> CSS processing -> Asset optimization -> Code splitting -> Bundling -> Minification -> Production output generation.
1.2 Understanding Modules and Dependency Graphs

Students will understand entry points, static imports, dynamic imports, dependency graphs, module resolution, circular dependencies, third-party package dependencies, and how unused modules can be removed.
1.3 Understanding Bundlers

Study the roles of Vite, Rollup, Webpack, and esbuild: module bundling, tree shaking, dead-code elimination, minification, code splitting, asset hashing, dependency optimization, and chunk generation.
1.4 Tree Shaking and Dead-Code Elimination
Tree shaking removes unused code from the final production bundle when ES modules and side-effect configuration allow static analysis.
1.5 Development Build vs Production Build

Development builds prioritize developer productivity; production builds prioritize smaller download sizes, faster execution, optimized assets, efficient caching, reduced debugging overhead, and stable delivery.

Practical exercise: Create a small React application containing multiple components and dependencies. Inspect its dependency graph and production output, identify unnecessary code and compare the development and production builds.
2.1 Understanding Vite Architecture
Understand Vite's development server, native ES module development workflow, dependency pre-bundling, plugin system, production build pipeline, and build preview.
2.2 Understanding vite.config.js
Configuration areas: plugins, dev server settings, port, host, path aliases, base paths, output directories, source maps, asset handling, build targets, and dependency optimization.
2.3 Environment-Specific Configuration
Organize separate settings for local development, testing, staging, and production without leaking dev configs to production.
2.4 Production Build Generation
Run npm run build, inspect generated assets, resolve missing dependencies, investigate build warnings, and preview the production build locally.
2.5 Build Optimization and Chunk Management
Understand vendor chunks, application chunks, route-based chunks, dynamic imports, lazy loading, manual chunk configuration, dependency duplication, and chunk size warnings.
Practical exercise: Configure a React application using Vite, organize its environment settings, implement route-based code splitting, generate a production build and inspect its output.
3.1 Understanding Environment Variables

VITE_API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787
VITE_APP_ENV=development
const API_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL;
3.2 Development, Staging and Production Environments
Development is for local coding/testing; Staging validates production-like behavior; Production serves actual users.
3.3 Environment Files in Vite
Understand .env, .env.local, .env.development, .env.production, build modes, and variable precedence.
3.4 Public Configuration vs Secret Configuration

In Vite, variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to client-side bundles. Public API URLs, analytics IDs, and feature flags can be exposed; database passwords, private API keys, and auth signing secrets must never enter frontend code.
3.5 Application Configuration Architecture

Practical exercise: Configure a frontend application for development, staging and production. Verify that public configuration is correctly loaded and that private credentials never enter the frontend bundle.

sections.title: ESLint, Prettier and Code Quality Standards

blocks.text: 4.1 Understanding Code Quality
Readability, consistency, predictable behavior, reusability, low complexity, proper naming, limited duplication, clear responsibilities, and meaningful error handling.
4.2 Understanding ESLint
Identifies potential bugs, unused variables, React hook dependency problems, and enforces coding rules.
4.3 Understanding Prettier
Standardizes presentation (indentation, spacing, line breaks, quotes, JSX formatting). Prettier handles formatting while ESLint checks code quality and rules.
4.4 Integrating Code Quality Tools
Config files, editor integration, format/lint scripts, pre-commit checks, PR quality checks, and CI pipeline integration.
4.5 Professional Code Review Standards
Review for correctness, maintainability, security, accessibility, performance, reusability, naming, and component complexity.
Practical exercise: Configure ESLint and Prettier in a React project. Introduce common coding mistakes and formatting inconsistencies, then use automated tools to identify and resolve them.

sections.title: Frontend Project Structure and Maintainable Codebases

blocks.text: 5.1 Understanding Project Architecture
Organize entry points, pages/routes, components, feature modules, hooks, API services, utilities, state management, styles, assets, configuration, and tests.
5.2 Feature-Based vs Type-Based Folder Structures
Type-based structure groups by technical role (components/, pages/, hooks/, services/, utils/, styles/).
Feature-based structure groups by domain (features/authentication/, features/courses/, features/dashboard/, features/profile/, shared/, app/, assets/), improving scalability for large apps.
5.3 Separation of Concerns
Separate presentation logic, business logic, API communication, state management, routing, form validation, and shared utilities.
5.4 Reusable and Maintainable Components
Focus on clear responsibilities, composition, typed props, shared vs feature-specific components, reusable hooks, and dependency boundaries.
5.5 Managing a Growing Codebase
Manage large component collections, duplicate functionality, import organization, deprecated components, dead code, and technical documentation.
5.6 Architecture Documentation
Document folder structures, key components, routing, state decisions, API communication, auth flow, configuration, and deployment procedures.
Practical exercise: Take a poorly organized React project and restructure it into a maintainable feature-based architecture without changing its existing functionality or UI.
6.1 Understanding Component-Driven Development
Build and validate independent UI components (Button, Input, CourseCard, Progress, Nav, Dialog, Alert) in isolation before assembling full pages.
6.2 Understanding Storybook Architecture
Storybook setup, story files, component previews, documentation, and state stories (Primary, Secondary, Disabled, Loading, Destructive, Sizes).
6.3 Component Variations and Controls
Preview course cards across different titles, instructors, thumbnails, progress values, and completed/in-progress states without launching the full app.
6.4 Interaction and Accessibility Testing
Use Storybook for interaction testing, keyboard navigation checks, accessibility checks, and visual regression testing.
6.5 Maintaining a Component Library
Document component purpose, props, variations, expected behavior, accessibility requirements, usage examples, and design constraints.

Practical exercise: Create a small Storybook component library containing buttons, inputs, course cards, modals and progress indicators. Document different states and demonstrate how other developers can reuse the components.

sections.title: Working with UI Libraries and Component Systems

blocks.text: 7.1 Understanding UI Libraries
Established ecosystems (Material UI, Ant Design, Chakra UI, Radix UI) provide buttons, inputs, dialogs, dropdowns, tables, tabs, and form controls.
7.2 Understanding Component Systems
Compare full UI libraries, headless component libraries (behavior + a11y primitives without fixed styling), design systems, CSS frameworks, and utility-first systems.
7.3 Design Tokens and Consistent Styling
Primary/secondary colors, typography scales, spacing, border radius, shadows, breakpoints, and component dimensions.
7.4 Customization and Theming
Theme configuration, CSS variables, design tokens, variants, and dark/light themes without mixing incompatible UI systems.
7.5 Evaluating and Selecting UI Libraries
Evaluate accessibility, docs, customization, bundle size, maintenance, community, compatibility, licensing, and long-term suitability.
7.6 Avoiding Excessive Dependency on UI Libraries
Balance library reuse against abstraction risks and lock-in.

Practical exercise: Build a consistent application interface using a selected UI library or component system. Customize its theme, establish design tokens and implement reusable components that match a defined design specification.

sections.title: Production Deployment with Cloudflare Pages and Vercel

blocks.text: 8.1 Understanding Frontend Deployment
Develop locally -> Commit to Git -> Push to GitHub -> Connect host -> Configure build command & output directory -> Set env vars -> Build assets -> Publish -> Verify deployed app.
8.2 Understanding Cloudflare Pages
GitHub integration, build settings, env vars, preview deployments, production deployments, custom domains, HTTPS, deployment logs, and rollbacks.
8.3 Understanding Vercel
Git integration, framework detection, build settings, env vars, preview/production deployments, custom domains, build logs, and deployment history.
8.4 Single-Page Application Routing
Configure SPA fallback/rewrite rules so direct access or refresh on nested client routes (e.g. /courses/frontend/react) serves the SPA entry instead of a 404.
8.5 Domain and HTTPS Configuration
Custom domains, DNS records, apex/subdomain setup, HTTPS/SSL/TLS certificates, redirects, canonical URLs, and www vs non-www normalization.
8.6 Preview and Production Deployments
Use preview deployments for PR reviews before publishing to production.

Practical exercise: Deploy the same React application to Cloudflare Pages and Vercel. Configure production and preview environments, connect a custom domain and verify direct access to nested application routes.

sections.title: CDN Integration, Asset Delivery and Cache Management

blocks.text: 9.1 Understanding Content Delivery Networks
Origin servers, edge locations, cache hits/misses, latency reduction, asset delivery, and cache invalidation.
9.2 Static Asset Optimization
Optimize images, SVGs, fonts, CSS, JS, icons, and downloadable documents.
9.3 Browser Caching and HTTP Cache Headers
Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified, Expires, max-age, s-maxage, no-cache, no-store, immutable, and revalidation.
9.4 Cache Versioning and Cache Invalidation
Content-hashed filenames (app.a83f21.js), fingerprinting, CDN purge operations, and HTML entry revalidation.
9.5 Cache Strategy Design
Resource | Typical caching approach
Hashed JavaScript files | Long-lived immutable caching
Hashed CSS files | Long-lived immutable caching
HTML entry document | Revalidation or short caching
Frequently changing API data | Application-specific caching
Sensitive private data | No shared public caching
Static public images | Long-lived caching when versioned
9.6 CDN Performance Troubleshooting
Investigate unexpected cache misses, stale asset delivery, wrong cache headers, broken static resources, origin failures, and invalidation issues.
Practical exercise: Configure caching for a deployed frontend application, inspect HTTP response headers, verify CDN behavior and implement an asset versioning strategy.
10.1 Understanding Continuous Integration
Automated PR checks: dependency installation, linting, type checking, unit tests, integration tests, production builds, and security/dependency checks.
10.2 Understanding Continuous Delivery and Deployment
Continuous Delivery prepares validated releases requiring approval; Continuous Deployment releases validated changes automatically.
10.3 GitHub-Based CI/CD Workflows
Pull Request -> Install Dependencies -> ESLint -> Tests -> Production Build -> All checks pass? -> Deploy Preview -> Review -> Approve Production -> Deploy Release.
10.4 Branching and Release Strategies
Feature branches, dev branches, main/production branches, PRs, release branches, version tags, hotfix branches, and code reviews.
10.5 Automated Deployment Workflows
Automated previews, production deployments, build artifacts, env vars, secrets management, approvals, release history, and failure handling.
10.6 Release Management
Release notes, version numbers, change summaries, deployment verification, API compatibility awareness, rollback planning, and post-release monitoring.

Practical exercise: Create a GitHub Actions workflow that installs dependencies, runs linting, executes tests and builds the application. Connect it to a preview deployment and a production release workflow.
11.1 Understanding Production Errors
JS runtime exceptions, failed API requests, auth failures, rendering errors, component crashes, asset loading failures, browser compatibility issues, unhandled promise rejections.
11.2 Error Monitoring Systems
Platforms like Sentry capture error events, stack traces, error grouping, browser/device context, release tracking, source maps, and user-impact analysis.
11.3 React Error Boundaries
Error boundaries isolate rendering crashes but do not automatically catch event-handler or async callback errors.
11.4 Application Analytics
Track page views, navigation, feature usage, session duration, conversions, form completion, search, course engagement, and retention.
11.5 Performance Monitoring
Measure Core Web Vitals, page loads, JS execution, API latency, resource failures, slow interactions, and device/network differences.
11.6 Privacy and Responsible Analytics
Enforce data minimization, avoid collecting sensitive form data/PII, respect consent, and configure access controls and retention.
Practical exercise: Integrate an error-monitoring tool and analytics solution into a deployed React application. Trigger controlled errors, inspect reports and measure selected user interactions.
12.1 Understanding Production Debugging
Investigate using browser DevTools, console, network, performance, storage, source maps, error-monitoring dashboards, deployment logs, and API responses.
12.2 Debugging API and Network Problems
Diagnose HTTP 400, 401/403, 404, 429 rate limits, 500 errors, CORS failures, timeouts, invalid JSON, request cancellation, and expired auth.
12.3 Production-Only Bugs
Missing env vars, wrong API URLs, broken SPA routing, wrong asset paths, CORS issues, stale cached files, case-sensitive imports, build-only errors, and browser differences.
12.4 Understanding Rollback
Return to a previous known-good release using deployment history, release verification, hotfixes, and cache considerations.
12.5 Incident Response and Postmortems
Detect -> Determine impact -> Identify affected features -> Restore/Rollback -> Investigate root cause -> Permanent fix -> Verify -> Document lessons learned.
Practical exercise: Deploy an intentionally faulty release, identify the issue using browser and deployment logs, restore the previous version and document the incident.
13.1 Understanding Progressive Web Applications
Web-based delivery, installability, responsive UI, HTTPS, Web App Manifest, service worker integration, offline support, and update handling.
13.2 Web App Manifest

{
  "name": "Learning Platform",
  "short_name": "Learn",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#ffffff",
  "theme_color": "#111111"
}
13.3 Application Installation
Browser installability criteria, install prompts, home-screen installation, standalone display, icons, and platform differences.
13.4 PWA Capabilities
Offline access, push notifications (where permitted), background sync, local data access, shortcuts, and share APIs.
13.5 When to Use a PWA
Evaluate suitability for learning platforms, productivity tools, news, docs, and business dashboards.
Practical exercise: Convert a React application into an installable PWA. Create a manifest, configure its icons and verify installation behavior across supported browsers.
14.1 Understanding Service Workers
Background scripts running separately from the main page context that intercept network requests and enable caching/offline behavior over HTTPS (or localhost).
14.2 Service Worker Lifecycle
Registration -> Installation -> Waiting -> Activation -> Fetch event handling -> Updating -> Unregistration.
14.3 Cache Storage API
Open caches, add resources, store responses, match requests, delete outdated caches, and manage cache versions.
14.4 Caching Strategies
Cache First, Network First, Stale While Revalidate, Network Only, and Cache Only — choose based on freshness and sensitivity.
14.5 Designing Offline Experiences
Offline status indicators, downloaded lessons, cached app shell, retry actions, offline fallback pages, and safe pending sync.
14.6 Service Worker Update Management
Cache versioning, cleanup, new-worker detection, update prompts, and reload strategies.
14.7 Limitations and Risks
Storage limits, cache expiration, stale content, sync conflicts, auth expiration, sensitive data, and browser differences.

Practical exercise: Implement a service worker for the learning platform. Cache the application shell, create an offline fallback page and implement an appropriate caching strategy for public course resources.
15.1 Understanding Micro-Frontends
Divides large frontend applications (dashboard, catalogue, learning player, auth, admin) into independently developed/deployed sections owned by separate teams.
15.2 Monolithic Frontend vs Micro-Frontend
Compare single-app monolithic frontends with independently managed micro-frontend modules connected via defined boundaries.
15.3 Micro-Frontend Integration Approaches
Build-time integration, runtime integration, Module Federation, Web Components, JS-based integration, and iframe integration.
15.4 Shared Dependencies and Design Systems
Manage shared React versions, component libraries, design tokens, auth context, routing, events, and utilities.
15.5 Communication Between Micro-Frontends
Custom events, shared interfaces, routing conventions, data contracts, and error isolation.
15.6 Challenges and Trade-Offs

Deployment complexity, dependency duplication, shared-state issues, performance overhead, UI inconsistency, testing complexity, and version conflicts. Use modular monoliths when micro-frontends are unnecessary.

Practical exercise: Design a learning platform architecture with independently owned student dashboard, course catalogue and administration interfaces. Create an integration plan showing routing, shared components, communication and deployment boundaries.
16.1 Understanding Internationalization and Localization
Internationalization (i18n) designs apps to support multiple languages/regions without major rewrites; Localization (l10n) adapts an app for a specific language/region.
16.2 Managing Translated Content
Manage translation keys, resource files, default/fallback languages, dynamic values, and pluralization.
16.3 Internationalization Libraries
Use libraries like i18next + React hooks for detection, namespaces, resource loading, and fallbacks.
16.4 Dates, Numbers and Currency
Use standard browser APIs (Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat) for locale-aware dates, numbers, and currencies.
16.5 Right-to-Left Languages
Support RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew) with text/layout direction, logical CSS properties, icon alignment, and bidirectional content.
16.6 Localization Beyond Translation
Currency, units, time zones, date conventions, address formats, cultural conventions, localized media, and regional features.
Practical exercise: Add multiple-language support to the learning platform. Implement language switching, locale-based date and number formatting and an RTL-compatible layout.
17.1 Understanding Team-Based Frontend Development
Address code conflicts, inconsistent components, duplicate code, style drift, dependency mismatches, and unclear ownership.
17.2 Architecture Boundaries and Responsibilities
Application area | Responsibility
Authentication | Login, registration and session interfaces
Course catalogue | Course discovery, search and filtering
Learning environment | Lesson presentation and navigation
Student dashboard | Progress and learning overview
Administration | Management interfaces
17.3 Monorepo and Multi-Repository Architecture
Compare monorepos (shared packages, workspace management, coordinated builds) vs multi-repos (separate lifecycles, independent ownership).
17.4 Shared Components and Design Standards
Shared component libraries, design tokens, reusable hooks, coding/a11y standards, naming conventions, docs, and versioning.
17.5 Team Development Workflows
Feature branches, PR reviews, issue tracking, task ownership, conflict resolution, shared dev environments, CI, and release coordination.
17.6 Architecture Decisions and Documentation
Use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to capture the problem, options, chosen solution, rationale, and consequences.

Practical exercise: Design the frontend architecture and development workflow for a team of five developers building the learning platform. Define module ownership, shared components, branch strategy and code review requirements.
18.1 Understanding Technical Debt
Future maintenance cost caused by shortcuts, duplicate components, oversized files, repeated API logic, missing tests, or outdated libraries.
18.2 Identifying Maintainability Problems
God components, deep nesting, duplicated logic, unclear naming, tight coupling, untestable code, and excessive global state.
18.3 Understanding Refactoring
Improving internal structure without changing externally observable behavior (extracting functions, components, custom hooks, simplifying state and folders).
18.4 Safe Refactoring Techniques
Understand existing behavior -> verify/add tests -> plan small change -> refactor small area -> run tests -> compare behavior -> review quality -> document.
18.5 Managing Dependencies and Technical Debt
Handle outdated packages, deprecated APIs, unused libraries, CVEs, and breaking upgrades safely.
18.6 Building a Long-Term Maintenance Strategy
Track technical debt registers, prioritize maintenance, schedule refactoring, prevent regressions, and conduct periodic architecture reviews.

Practical exercise: Inspect an existing React application containing duplicated components, complex state handling and unnecessary dependencies. Prepare a technical debt report, refactor selected areas and demonstrate that the original functionality remains intact.
19.1 Understanding Project Requirements

Identify functional requirements (landing, registration/login, course discovery, course/module pages, dashboard, progress tracking) and non-functional requirements (responsive design, a11y, performance, security, maintainability, browser compatibility, reliability, scalability).
19.2 Identifying Users and User Journeys
Visitor -> Landing Page -> Course Discovery -> Course Details -> Register / Login -> Student Dashboard -> Open Course -> Start Learning -> Track Progress.
19.3 Frontend Architecture Design
Define entry point, routing, page structure, component hierarchy, shared UI, feature modules, state management, API services, auth flow, error handling, config, and tests.
19.4 Data and API Contract Planning

  "id": "frontend-101",

19.5 Wireframes and UI Planning
Plan landing page, auth screens, course catalogue, course detail, learning dashboard, module page, and progress UI.
19.6 Technology and Architecture Decisions
Area | Example technology
Frontend framework | React
Build tool | Vite
Language | JavaScript or TypeScript
Styling | Tailwind CSS or CSS
Routing | React Router
API integration | Fetch or Axios
Server-state management | TanStack Query
Testing | Vitest, React Testing Library and Playwright
Component documentation | Storybook
Deployment | Cloudflare Pages or Vercel
Version control | Git and GitHub
Practical deliverable: Project requirement document, user journeys, wireframes, application architecture diagram, folder structure, API contract plan and technology selection document.
20.1 Establishing the Design System
Define primary/secondary colors, typography, spacing, border radius, shadows, breakpoints, icons, button variants, form styles, and component states.
20.2 Creating the Application Foundation
Set up project, Vite config, entry point, global styles, routing, shared layouts, app config, and error boundaries.
20.3 Developing Reusable Components
Build Navbar, Footer, Sidebar, Buttons, Inputs, Dropdowns, Search bar, Course cards, Progress indicators, Modals, Notifications, and Pagination.
20.4 Developing Main Application Pages
Implement Landing page, Course catalogue, Course details, Student dashboard, and Learning interface.
20.5 Component State and Interactive Behavior
Dropdowns, search, pagination, active nav, modals, forms, loading skeletons, empty states, error states, and progress displays.
20.6 Design Consistency and Maintainability
Verify consistent component behavior across pages without duplicated styling or uncontrolled complexity.
Practical deliverable: A functional React frontend containing the major platform pages, shared components, application navigation and consistent design system.
21.1 Understanding Frontend and Backend Communication
Frontend presents UI and collects interactions; backend handles auth, profiles, courses, learning content, progress, and enrollments.
21.2 Creating an API Service Layer
21.3 Authentication API Integration
Integrate registration, login, session handling, expiration, logout, protected routes, and unauthorized responses while keeping backend authorization authoritative.
21.4 Server State and Client State
Separate server state (courses, progress) from client state (menus, tabs, modals).
21.5 Data Fetching and Synchronization
Implement loading, success, empty, and error states, refetching, caching, pagination, search, and invalidation.
21.6 Student Progress Integration
21.7 Handling Real-World API Problems
Handle network failures, invalid responses, expired sessions, 401/403, rate limits, slow responses, duplicate requests, and backend downtime.
Practical deliverable: A frontend integrated with authentication and course APIs, featuring session handling, protected experiences, reusable API services and synchronized application state.
22.1 Mobile-First Development
Design for smaller screens first using mobile-first CSS, breakpoints, Grid, Flexbox, fluid typography, and responsive images.
22.2 Cross-Device Layout Design
Verify mobile phones, tablets, laptops, and desktops for zero horizontal overflow, no overlap, proper scaling, and accessible menus.
22.3 Understanding Web Accessibility
Semantic HTML, accessible navigation, keyboard interaction, screen-reader support, focus management, contrast, labels, error messages, alt text, and headings.
22.4 WCAG Fundamentals
Apply Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust (POUR) principles across all interactive UI.
22.5 Accessible Forms and Interactive Components
Proper input labels, validation announcements, keyboard-operable dropdowns, accessible modals, visible focus states, and clear button names.
22.6 Accessibility and Responsive Testing
Verify via keyboard-only navigation, browser zoom, screen-reader checks, contrast analysis, automated accessibility tools, and multi-viewport checks.
Practical deliverable: A responsive learning platform that provides a consistent experience across supported devices and implements appropriate accessibility practices.
23.1 Understanding Frontend Testing Strategy
Combine unit testing, integration testing, and end-to-end testing.
23.2 Unit Testing
Test utilities, validation, transformations, reusable hooks, individual components, and conditional rendering.
23.3 Component and Integration Testing
Test forms + validation, buttons + state, components + API services, auth + protected routes, and course pages + progress.
23.4 End-to-End Testing
Landing -> Course catalogue -> Search -> Course details -> Login -> Student dashboard -> Learning module -> Verify progress display.
23.5 Testing Tools
Vitest, React Testing Library, Playwright, accessibility testing utilities, and Browser DevTools.
23.6 Performance Profiling
Measure browser rendering, React rendering, JS execution, network requests, bundle size, memory, long tasks, and layout shifts.
23.7 Frontend Performance Optimization
Route-based code splitting, lazy loading, dynamic imports, image/font optimization, bundle reduction, caching, and efficient rendering.
23.8 Core Web Vitals
Measure and improve LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness), and CLS (visual stability).
23.9 SEO and Frontend Quality
Verify titles, meta descriptions, canonical URLs, semantic HTML, structured data, crawlable links, social metadata, sitemaps, robots directives, and mobile usability.
Practical deliverable: A complete testing suite for major platform workflows, a test report, a performance report and an optimization record showing improvements and remaining limitations.
24.1 Production Readiness Review
Inspect functionality, build success, env config, auth, APIs, error handling, responsiveness, a11y, security, SEO, performance, and browser compatibility.
24.2 Production Build and Release Preparation
Review code quality, resolve lint issues, run automated tests, verify production build, check env vars, inspect assets, verify API config, and prepare release docs.
24.3 Production Deployment
Deploy to Cloudflare Pages or Vercel with production build settings, env vars, custom domain, HTTPS, SPA routing fallback, CDN, and cache rules.
24.4 Post-Deployment Verification
Test homepage, direct nested routes, registration/login, catalogue, search/filtering, course details, dashboard, APIs, progress, responsiveness, error handling, and browsers in production.
24.5 Monitoring and Maintenance
Configure error monitoring, performance monitoring, analytics, deployment history, release tracking, incident investigation, and rollback procedures.
24.6 Final Technical Evaluation
Evaluate architecture, code organization, reusability, API integration, state, auth, responsiveness, a11y, testing, performance, SEO, deployment, and documentation.
24.7 Technical Presentation
Present overview, problem, user journeys, architecture, component design, API integration, security, testing, performance, deployment, challenges, and future improvements.
Final deliverable: A deployed frontend application, its complete source code, architecture documentation, automated test reports and a technical presentation.
Final industry capstone
Students will engineer a complete frontend for a modern learning platform, applying the concepts from all previous modules and the production engineering practices introduced in Module 14.
Project overview

Build a frontend application where visitors can discover educational courses, register, log in, access a student dashboard, open courses and modules, and monitor their learning progress, integrated with authentication, course, and progress APIs.
Project requirements

1. Responsive Landing Page and Course Discovery: Navigation bar, hero section, platform intro, featured courses, categories, benefits, CTAs, footer, and responsive navigation without horizontal overflow.

2. Student Registration and Login Interface: Registration & login forms, email/password validation, error messages, loading states, success/failure states, logout, session handling, and protected experiences aligned with the auth API contract.

3. Course Catalogue with Search, Filters and Pagination: Course cards, thumbnails, titles/descriptions, categories, difficulty levels, search, filtering, sorting, pagination, loading/empty/error states.
4. Individual Course and Module Pages: Course overview, description, learning objectives, module list, course navigation, and readable module/lesson learning interface.
5. Interactive Learning Dashboard: Student info, enrolled courses, course progress, recent activity, completed modules, continue-learning actions, and API-backed statistics.
6. Student Progress and Completion Interfaces: Course/module/lesson completion status, progress indicators, and backend-synchronized updates.
7. Reusable Component Architecture and Design System: Navbar, buttons, inputs, cards, progress bars, dropdowns, modals, notifications, skeletons, and error messages with consistent tokens.
8. API Integration and Data Synchronization: Auth, catalogue, course details, learning content, profile, enrollment, and progress with loading/success/empty/error handling.
9. Form Validation and Error Handling: Required/email/password validation, invalid input messages, submission loading, API/network errors, accessible error announcements.

10. Protected User Experiences and Appropriate Session Handling: Protected routes, auth status handling, login redirects, logout, session expiration, 401 handling, with backend remaining the authorization authority.

11. Accessibility and Cross-Device Compatibility: Mobile-responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, semantic HTML, form labels, headings, screen-reader controls, contrast, focus indicators, accessible dialogs, responsive images.
12. Unit, Integration and End-to-End Tests: Unit tests (utilities, validation, components), integration tests (components + API + forms + state), and E2E tests (discovery, auth, dashboard).
13. SEO and Performance Optimization: Titles, descriptions, canonicals, semantic structure, headings, image optimization, lazy loading, code splitting, bundle optimization, caching, Core Web Vitals.

14. Production Deployment with Monitoring: Production build, env config, hosting, custom domain, HTTPS, SPA routing fallback, CDN/cache rules, post-release verification, error/performance monitoring, rollback readiness.
Recommended Project Development Workflow
Phase 1 — Requirements and Planning: Requirements, target users, user journeys, wireframes, feature scope, API contracts.
Phase 2 — Architecture and Setup: React, Vite, routing, folder structure, design tokens, env vars, shared components.
Phase 3 — Core UI Development: Landing page, auth screens, course catalogue, course pages, student dashboard.
Phase 4 — API and State Integration: Auth, courses, progress APIs, data fetching, state, error handling.
Phase 5 — Responsive Design and Accessibility: Mobile/desktop adaptation, keyboard access, semantic structure, a11y validation.
Phase 6 — Testing and Optimization: Automated tests, performance profiling, asset optimization, SEO verification.
Phase 7 — Deployment and Monitoring: Production env, deployment, live workflow verification, monitoring setup.
Phase 8 — Final Review and Presentation: Documentation, test reports, demonstration, architectural defense.

UI documentation | Wireframes, design system and reusable component documentation
API documentation | API endpoints, request/response expectations and integration details
Testing reports | Unit, integration and end-to-end test results
Performance report | Measurements, identified issues and optimization results
Accessibility report | Testing results and identified improvements
Deployment documentation | Build configuration, environment setup and deployment procedure
Deployed application | Working production frontend

sections.title: Final Learning Outcomes and Completion Standard

blocks.text: Final Learning Outcomes
After successfully completing Module 14, students should be able to:
Understand modern frontend build systems and production bundling.
Configure Vite for development and production.
Manage environment variables and application configuration securely.
Establish professional code-quality standards with ESLint and Prettier.
Design maintainable frontend project architectures.
Document reusable components with Storybook.
Work with UI libraries and design systems.
Deploy React applications using Cloudflare Pages and Vercel.
Optimize CDN delivery and browser caching.
Implement CI/CD pipelines and release workflows.
Monitor frontend errors and application performance.
Debug production problems and perform rollbacks.
Build installable Progressive Web Applications.
Implement service workers and offline functionality.
Understand micro-frontend architecture and its trade-offs.
Implement internationalization and localization.
Organize frontend development for large engineering teams.
Identify technical debt and safely refactor codebases.
Plan complete frontend application architecture.
Build reusable, responsive and accessible production interfaces.
Integrate frontend applications with backend APIs.
Implement testing and performance optimization strategies.
Deploy and maintain production frontend applications.
Present a complete industry-style frontend engineering project.

Module completion standard: Students should not consider the module complete simply because the application runs locally. They must demonstrate that their learning platform is properly structured, integrated, tested, accessible, responsive, deployed and documented.
This completes the Modern Web & Frontend Engineering course's journey from frontend fundamentals to professional production engineering.
